← Vocal Exercises

About these exercises

The five training sections contain original note arrangements and instructions built around common singing tasks. They are not song transcriptions or reproductions of a named teaching program.

Each section offers a practice focus, not a test of your register. A piano cannot confirm whether you are using chest voice, mix, head voice or falsetto. These labels can also be used differently by different teachers.

Choose a comfortable range before playing. The General Warmups presets are broad pitch limits. Training presets are narrower practice choices, not targets you must reach in every exercise. For chest voice and belt foundations, begin with a small range near comfortable speaking pitch. Adjust the limits whenever the sound stops feeling easy.

Belting exercises here introduce clear, speech-like sounds at moderate volume. They do not teach full-power or high belting on their own. A qualified singing teacher can give feedback on that coordination.

Breathe whenever you need to, even if the piano continues. Hold key repeats a key, not your breath. Use More options to add breathing time. Stop for pain, strain or increasing hoarseness. Persistent symptoms need professional assessment.

Ranges by practice focus

Chest presets finish at B♭3 for baritone and C4 for tenor. Common classical teaching landmarks put the first transition around B♭3–B3 for baritones and C4–D4 for heavier and lyric tenors, with lighter tenors often higher. Second transitions are commonly around E♭4–E4 and F4–G4 respectively. These are approximate landmarks, not universal register boundaries or a voice-type test. See Karyn O’Connor’s registration overview.

Mix presets span A3–F4 (baritone) and C4–A4 (tenor), bracketing the transition area. Shorter patterns keep every note inside those limits. Your changes are remembered separately for each section and voice type.

Head/falsetto presets are E4–F5 and F4–G5. These are app practice choices, not published average ranges for baritones and tenors. Phonational Frequency Ranges of Adults measures full modal-to-falsetto capability, not a comfortable daily exercise range. A voice label alone cannot predict your upper limit. Lower the preset if needed, and use light coordination above your comfortable head range.

Belt foundations start at C3–E4 or D3–G4. C5 is this app’s upper adjustment limit, not a safe target for every man or a biological ceiling. Efficiency depends on the individual voice and coordination, as discussed in Robert Edwin’s Belt Is Legit. Never force a higher pitch because the slider allows it.

Breathing timers

Six exercises use unpitched clicks and visible phase counts. Seconds-based timers stay fixed when tempo changes. Bar-based timers use four beats per bar at your chosen BPM. Each has three rounds, including normal breathing between efforts. The timings are short practice designs for this app, not a validated clinical protocol or endurance targets. There are no breath-holding phases. Breathe early, pause, or stop if uncomfortable or lightheaded. The remaining four exercises use piano for sustained vocal tone.

Counting scales and intervals

The expanding scale builds 1, then 121, then 12321, continuing to the octave. It then mirrors from 8, through 878 and 87678, down to the bottom note and back. One beat between groups gives a breathing space. The chart shows the current group. This common counting exercise is documented in the Philharmonia vocal exercise guide. This app generates its own piano performance.

The Intervals bank covers the 13 chromatic distances from unison to octave. Each alternates low and high notes. Rock Runs contains 10 original melodic studies, with no song transcriptions or requirement to add distortion.

Technique references

The general exercise types were checked against these educational resources. The pitch arrangements and short prompts in this app were written for this app. These sources do not endorse the app.

  • Duke Voice Care Center: Ideas for Vocal Exercises
  • NATS: Music Theater Resources
  • ASHA: Voice Disorders, including semi-occluded vocal exercises

This is a practice tool, not voice therapy.

Piano credits

Scales and longer runs

Agility patterns use original arrangements of repeating three-, four-, and five-note groups, thirds, scales, and arpeggios. These are general practice forms, not song transcriptions. Pentatonic patterns are collected together, including those previously listed under genres. All genre banks have now been consolidated by pitch content. Short turns, trills, grace-note approaches, and melismatic phrases are in Agility. These are original exercises, not transcriptions of the examples in Jaco Explains’ overview of riffs and runs. Piano demonstrates discrete pitches. Slides and bends now use a continuous synth reference. Whistle-register technique is not modeled. Melodic minor uses raised sixth and seventh degrees ascending and natural minor descending.

Practice-form references: Duke Voice Care Center vocal exercises and ABRSM scale and arpeggio patterns.

Comfortable sustain timer

Use a normal breath and an easy sung note. The timer can continue beyond a minute, but that is not a goal or a recommended minimum. Stop before strain, dizziness, or an urgent need for air. This is not a breath-holding test. See NIDCD voice-care guidance.
